group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 43-year-old man presented to the emergency department late this afternoon after two days of pleuritic left-sided chest discomfort, low-grade fever, and a cough that evolved from a dry throat tickle into scant rust-colored sputum this morning; he also noted a vague sense of abdominal fullness when he tried to inhale deeply but denied frank dyspnea at rest. The patient lives with his spouse in a second-floor apartment, works as an accountant, and normally climbs one flight of stairs several times per day without limitation. He contacted his cardiologist by telephone when his home blood-pressure cuff registered a pulse persistently above 120 beats per minute while he sat at his desk, and he was advised to come for evaluation. His medical history is notable for a dilated cardiomyopathy related to childhood viral myocarditis with an ejection fraction last documented at 35 % six months ago; guideline-directed medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, and a morning dose of furosemide 20 mg. In addition, he carries a diagnosis of stage 3b chronic kidney impairment attributed to long-standing hypertension; baseline serum creatinine has ranged between 2.0 and 2.3 mg/dL, and he follows nephrology every quarter but has never required dialysis. There is no record of prior stroke, transient ischemic attack, chronic liver condition, or any malignant disease, and he has never undergone radiation or cytotoxic therapy. He quit cigarette smoking eight years ago after a fifteen-pack-year exposure, drinks beer socially on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. He had taken his usual morning medications but no antipyretics, antibiotics, or inhalers before arrival. Emergency medical services transported him from home without oxygen or intravenous fluids so that baseline measurements could be captured in the department. On arrival he was seated upright on the stretcher, speaking in complete sentences, oriented to date, location, and circumstances, and able to recount the sequence of events without difficulty. Skin was warm and faintly diaphoretic; capillary refill was brisk, and there was no peripheral edema beyond the trace ankle pitting that has been stable for years. Pre-intervention vital signs recorded orally showed a temperature of 100.2 °F, a regular pulse of 127 beats per minute, automated blood pressure 120/76 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute with unlabored excursions, and fingertip oxygen saturation of 93 % while breathing room air at sea-level altitude. Neck veins were noted 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, unchanged from cardiology documentation. Cardiac auscultation revealed a tachycardic S1 and S2 with a soft third heart sound consistent with his baseline; no new murmurs or pericardial rub were identified. Pulmonary examination demonstrated diminished breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion over the lower half of the left posterior thorax with faint late-inspiratory crackles just superior to that zone; the right lung transmitted vesicular sounds throughout without wheezes. Abdomen was soft and nontender, liver span percussed at 10 cm, and there was no splenomegaly. Neurologic screen showed equal, reactive pupils, symmetric facial movements, 5/5 strength in all extremities, intact sensation, and steady finger-to-nose testing. Bedside capillary glucose measured 101 mg/dL. Venous and radial arterial samples were drawn within ten minutes of triage before any medications, flushes, or supplemental oxygen were administered. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 121 mEq/L, potassium 4.3 mEq/L, chloride 97 mEq/L, bicarbonate 26 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 53 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, consistent with his known renal profile but showing new hyponatremia. Complete blood count revealed white blood cells 13.9 × 10⁹/L with 86 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 41 %, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, and platelets 212 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas on ambient air showed pH 7.62, PaCO₂ 29 mm Hg, PaO₂ 71 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, and a base excess of +2, indicating a primary respiratory alkalosis likely driven by pain-associated hyperventilation with mild hypoxemia. Serum lactate was 1.4 mmol/L. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any therapy demonstrated a heterogeneous consolidation involving the lingular and adjacent lower-lobe segments on the left with a curvilinear meniscus blunting the left costophrenic angle, suggesting a small free-flowing pleural fluid collection; cardiac silhouette and mediastinum were unchanged from an image six months earlier, and the right lung field was clear. Electrocardiography performed simultaneously showed sinus tachycardia at 125 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T changes identical to prior tracings and no acute ischemia. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an expectorated sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any antimicrobial or diuretic therapy. At the time this narrative is entered the patient remains seated comfortably on room air, has received no antipyretics, no intravenous crystalloids, no bronchodilators, and no antibiotics, thereby preserving the physiologic and laboratory values detailed above as his untreated baseline for ongoing risk stratification and management planning.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and imaging points at presentation.
- Demographics: male, age 43 → 43 points. Lives at home, not in a nursing home → 0.
- Comorbidities: heart failure with ejection fraction 35% → 10; stage 3b chronic kidney disease → 10. No neoplastic, liver, or cerebrovascular disease → 0 each.
- Examination: pulse 127/min (≥125) → 10. Alert mentation, respiratory rate 18/min (<30), systolic pressure 120 mm Hg (≥90), and temperature 100.2 °F (37.9 °C, neither <35 nor ≥40) → 0 each.
- Labs: BUN 53 mg/dL (≥30) → 20; sodium 121 mEq/L (<130) → 20. Arterial pH 7.62 (not <7.35), glucose 101 mg/dL (<250), hematocrit 41% (≥30%), and room-air PaO₂ 71 mm Hg (≥60) with saturation 93% (≥90%) → 0 each.
- Imaging: left pleural effusion → 10.
Sum: 43 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 123 (PSI class IV).
Final answer: 123
